--- title: "Underfitting and overfitting" description: "A model can fail on new data by being too rigid or too flexible. The two failures leave different signs in its two errors, and on the survey the flexible one costs far more." order: 2 categories: [generalisation] --- ## Two ways to fail on new data [Decision trees](../03-supervised-learning/decision-trees.qmd) chose a tree's depth on validation sites: as the tree grew deeper, its error on those sites fell a little and then rose. This page names the two ends of that curve. A model can be too rigid to follow the pattern in the data, or so flexible that it follows the noise as well, and the two failures need opposite fixes. Setting the model's training error beside its error on new data, the two errors of [the previous page](training-versus-new-data.qmd), tells you which one you have. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The U-shaped error curve and its two failures Before it sees any data, a model is limited to a family of shapes. A straight line can only be a straight line; a tree with four leaves can only give four different predictions. How wide that family is, is the model's **flexibility**. - **Underfitting** is a model too rigid to follow the pattern. It misses the training data and new data by about as much, so its two errors are both high and close together. It is not fooled by noise; it simply cannot bend enough. - **Overfitting** is a model flexible enough to follow the noise as well as the signal. Its training error is low and its error on new data high, and the wide gap between them is the sign. As flexibility grows, the training error keeps falling. The error on new data falls while the model is still picking up the pattern, reaches a lowest point, then rises as the model fits more and more noise. Plotted against flexibility, it makes a U, called the **U-shaped error curve**. The best setting lies at its lowest point, between the two failures, and only the error on new data shows where. ::: {.diagram} ![An underfitted model is too rigid to follow the pattern, so both its errors are high and close together. An overfitted model bends through every point, so its training error is low but its error on new data is high. The training error falls all the way; the error on new data has a lowest point in between.](img/underfitting-and-overfitting.svg){fig-alt="Three small panels show the same eleven points with a hump-shaped pattern. Too rigid, underfitting: a straight line that misses the hump. In between: a smooth curve that follows the hump. Too flexible, overfitting: a zigzag through every point. Below, a wide panel plots two errors against flexibility. The training error falls steadily to zero. The error on new data falls a little, reaches its lowest point, then rises. On the left, the underfitting zone, both errors are high and close together. On the right, the overfitting zone, the training error is low and the error on new data high, with a wide gap between them."} ::: Both failures show up as a model that predicts badly, so they are easily confused, yet the fixes go in opposite directions. An underfitted model needs more flexibility or better inputs. An overfitted one needs less flexibility or more data, and [Regularisation](regularisation.qmd) offers a third way to hold it back. ## Worked example The data and split are those of [the previous page](training-versus-new-data.qmd): the training sites are split 20 times at random, by site, into fitting sites and new sites, and each error is averaged over the 20 splits. The test sites are still unused. The setting varied here is a tree's **minimum node size**, `min_n`: the smallest group of stations the tree may split into two. [Decision trees](../03-supervised-learning/decision-trees.qmd) varied the depth instead. Set large, it lets the tree split only a few times; set to 2, it lets the tree go on splitting until each leaf holds a single station. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) # 20 random splits of the training sites: fitting sites and new sites splits <- group_mc_cv(train, group = site_id, prop = 0.75, times = 20) predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season tree_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) # The depth limit is set high so that min_n alone sets the size of the tree. tree_model <- function(min_n) { decision_tree(mode = "regression", tree_depth = 30, min_n = min_n, cost_complexity = 0) } leaves_of <- function(fitted) sum(extract_fit_engine(fitted)$frame$var == "") ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train = survey.iloc[train_rows] tree_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) # 20 random splits of the training sites: fitting sites and new sites splitter = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=20, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) splits = list(splitter.split(train, groups=train["site_id"])) # rpart also keeps every leaf at a third of min_n or more; this matches it. def tree_model(min_n): return DecisionTreeRegressor(min_samples_split=min_n, min_samples_leaf=max(1, round(min_n / 3)), random_state=123) ``` ::: ::: ### Node size sets how closely a tree follows temperature To see what the setting does, three trees are fitted to all the training stations with temperature as their only input, so that each tree's predictions can be drawn as a line. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} temperature_recipe <- recipe(abundance ~ temperature_c, data = train) |> step_impute_median(temperature_c) three_sizes <- c(300, 50, 2) one_input <- map(three_sizes, \(n) { workflow(temperature_recipe, tree_model(n)) |> fit(train) }) tibble(min_n = three_sizes, leaves = map_int(one_input, leaves_of)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| min_n| leaves| |-----:|------:| | 300| 4| | 50| 20| | 2| 414|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} one_input = { n: Pipeline([("recipe", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("model", tree_model(n))]) .fit(train[["temperature_c"]], train["abundance"]) for n in [300, 50, 2] } pd.DataFrame({"min_n": list(one_input), "leaves": [m["model"].get_n_leaves() for m in one_input.values()]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | min_n | leaves | |--------:|---------:| | 300 | 4 | | 50 | 20 | | 2 | 396 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} grid <- tibble(temperature_c = seq(min(train$temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE), max(train$temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE), length.out = 1500)) lines <- map2(one_input, three_sizes, \(fitted, n) { grid |> mutate(.pred = predict(fitted, grid)$.pred, min_n = n) }) |> list_rbind() labeller <- \(n) paste0("A node needs ", n, " stations\n", one_leaves[match(as.numeric(n), three_sizes)], " leaves") ggplot(train, aes(temperature_c, abundance)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 1, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_step(data = lines, aes(y = .pred), colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], linewidth = 0.7) + facet_wrap(~ factor(min_n, levels = three_sizes), labeller = as_labeller(labeller)) + labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Abundance") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Three trees fitted to the training stations with temperature as their only input. A node must hold at least 300, 50 or 2 stations before it may split. The grey points are the stations.](underfitting-and-overfitting_files/figure-html/fig-one-input-1.png){#fig-one-input fig-alt='Three panels of abundance against temperature, each with grey points for the training stations and an orange step line for one tree\'s predictions. Left, a node needs 300 stations to split and the tree has 4 leaves, so the line has a few broad, level steps. Centre, 50 stations and 20 leaves, a staircase with more steps that rises and falls across the temperature range. Right, 2 stations and 414 leaves, a dense comb of narrow spikes reaching up to the highest catches.' width=1800} ::: ::: ::: The first tree has 4 leaves and gives the same prediction across wide bands of temperature: it can show only the coarsest rise and fall. The second, with 20 leaves, follows more of the pattern. The third has 414 leaves and jumps up to meet nearly every large catch. Those catches are mostly luck, and a new station at the same temperature is unlikely to repeat them. ### Sweeping the node size draws the U-shaped curve Now the trees use all six inputs, as in [Decision trees](../03-supervised-learning/decision-trees.qmd). For each split, trees with 12 minimum node sizes, from 300 down to 2, are fitted to the fitting sites and scored on the fitting stations and on the new sites. Predicting the fitting stations' average count everywhere gives a baseline. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sizes <- c(300, 200, 130, 80, 50, 30, 20, 13, 8, 5, 3, 2) score_split <- function(s) { fitting <- analysis(s) new <- assessment(s) map(sizes, \(n) { fitted <- workflow(tree_recipe, tree_model(n)) |> fit(fitting) tibble(min_n = n, leaves = leaves_of(fitted), training = rmse_vec(fitting$abundance, predict(fitted, fitting)$.pred), average = rmse_vec(new$abundance, rep(mean(fitting$abundance), nrow(new))), new = rmse_vec(new$abundance, predict(fitted, new)$.pred)) }) |> list_rbind() } sweep <- map(splits$splits, score_split) |> list_rbind() |> group_by(min_n) |> summarise(across(c(leaves, training, average, new), mean)) |> mutate(gap = new - training) |> arrange(desc(min_n)) sweep |> select(-average) |> mutate(across(-min_n, \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| min_n| leaves| training| new| gap| |-----:|------:|--------:|----:|-----:| | 300| 3.00| 4.69| 4.65| -0.04| | 200| 4.00| 4.58| 4.58| 0.00| | 130| 5.50| 4.51| 4.61| 0.10| | 80| 9.45| 4.37| 4.66| 0.29| | 50| 14.45| 4.21| 4.68| 0.48| | 30| 25.85| 3.89| 4.70| 0.81| | 20| 37.30| 3.72| 4.80| 1.08| | 13| 61.30| 3.32| 5.09| 1.77| | 8| 97.25| 2.63| 5.59| 2.96| | 5| 152.75| 1.94| 5.92| 3.99| | 3| 252.80| 0.71| 6.16| 5.46| | 2| 311.80| 0.00| 6.21| 6.21|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} sizes = [300, 200, 130, 80, 50, 30, 20, 13, 8, 5, 3, 2] rmse = root_mean_squared_error rows = [] for fit_rows, new_rows in splits: fitting, new = train.iloc[fit_rows], train.iloc[new_rows] for n in sizes: fitted = (Pipeline([("recipe", tree_recipe), ("model", tree_model(n))]) .fit(fitting[predictors], fitting["abundance"])) rows.append({ "min_n": n, "leaves": fitted["model"].get_n_leaves(), "training": rmse(fitting["abundance"], fitted.predict(fitting[predictors])), "average": rmse(new["abundance"], np.full(len(new), fitting["abundance"].mean())), "new": rmse(new["abundance"], fitted.predict(new[predictors])), }) sweep = (pd.DataFrame(rows).groupby("min_n", as_index=False).mean() .assign(gap=lambda d: d["new"] - d["training"]) .sort_values("min_n", ascending=False)) sweep.drop(columns="average").round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | min_n | leaves | training | new | gap | |--------:|---------:|-----------:|------:|------:| | 300 | 2.75 | 4.16 | 4.37 | 0.21 | | 200 | 4 | 4.08 | 4.3 | 0.22 | | 130 | 5.6 | 4.02 | 4.34 | 0.32 | | 80 | 8.8 | 3.88 | 4.38 | 0.51 | | 50 | 15.05 | 3.7 | 4.44 | 0.75 | | 30 | 24.6 | 3.51 | 4.59 | 1.08 | | 20 | 37.05 | 3.27 | 4.71 | 1.44 | | 13 | 58.95 | 2.95 | 4.94 | 2 | | 8 | 92.55 | 2.53 | 5.14 | 2.61 | | 5 | 148.35 | 1.8 | 5.51 | 3.71 | | 3 | 243.55 | 0.69 | 5.8 | 5.11 | | 2 | 297.35 | 0 | 5.86 | 5.86 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sweep |> pivot_longer(c(training, new), names_to = "set", values_to = "rmse") |> mutate(set = factor(set, levels = c("training", "new"), labels = c("Fitting stations", "New sites"))) |> ggplot(aes(leaves, rmse, colour = set)) + geom_hline(yintercept = baseline, linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_vline(xintercept = best$leaves, linetype = "dotted") + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2) + annotate("text", x = 1.3, y = baseline + 0.3, label = "predict the average", hjust = 0, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], size = 3.4) + scale_x_log10() + labs(x = "Leaves in the tree (log scale)", y = "RMSE (individuals)", colour = NULL, title = "Training error falls all the way; the error on new sites does not") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![RMSE on the fitting stations and on new sites against the number of leaves in the tree, averaged over 20 splits of the training sites. The dashed line is the error of predicting the fitting stations' average count; the dotted line marks the lowest error on new sites.](underfitting-and-overfitting_files/figure-html/fig-sweep-1.png){#fig-sweep fig-alt='Two lines of RMSE against the number of leaves on a logarithmic axis from 1 to about 312. The training line starts at 4.69 with about 3 leaves and falls ever faster to zero at the right. The line for new sites starts at 4.65, dips to its lowest point, 4.58, at about 4 leaves, marked by a dotted line, then climbs to 6.21. A dashed line at 4.83 marks predicting the average; the line for new sites crosses above it between 37 and 61 leaves.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: ### Too much flexibility costs more than too little **The rigid end.** With a node size of 300, the largest here, the tree has about 3 leaves. Its training error is 4.69 and its error on new sites 4.65, within 0.04 of each other. That is the sign of underfitting: both errors high and close together. A tree that never splits at all would predict the average count everywhere, the dashed line at 4.83. **The lowest point.** The error on new sites is lowest, at 4.58, for a node size of 200, which gives trees of about 4 leaves. That is better than the baseline, but only by 0.25: the counts are noisy, and even the best tree leaves most of their variation unexplained. **The flexible end.** With a node size of 2, the tree has about 312 leaves and a training error of zero. Its error on new sites is 6.21, worse than predicting the average. Trees of about 37 leaves still beat the baseline; at about 61 leaves and beyond, using the inputs at all does more harm than good. The training error gives no sign of that point: it falls smoothly through it. **The two costs are lopsided.** On new sites, a tree that never splits, the most rigid there can be, is 0.25 worse than the best one. The most flexible is 1.63 worse, about seven times as much. With counts this noisy there is much more noise to fit than signal to miss, so on these data too much flexibility is the costlier mistake. The best node size here was found by averaging over 20 splits of the training sites. [Hyperparameter selection](hyperparameter-selection.qmd) turns that idea into the standard method, cross-validation, and shows why a single split is not enough. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A model's **flexibility** is how wide a family of shapes it can take. Too little and it **underfits**; too much and it **overfits**. - Underfitting shows as two errors that are both high and close together. Overfitting shows as a low training error and a much higher error on new data. - The training error falls with every gain in flexibility, so it cannot locate the best setting. The error on new data traces the **U-shaped error curve**, and its lowest point, in between, is the target. - On the survey, a tree with a station in every leaf did worse on new sites than predicting the average, and the cost of too much flexibility was several times the cost of too little. - The fixes are opposite: more flexibility or better inputs for underfitting; less flexibility, regularisation or more data for overfitting. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Sweep the depth instead, as [Decision trees](../03-supervised-learning/decision-trees.qmd) did. In `tree_model()`, write `tree_depth = min_n, min_n = 2` in place of `tree_depth = 30, min_n = min_n`, then set `sizes <- 1:15`. Averaged over 20 splits, is the lowest point at the same depth that one validation split chose in section 3? 2. Give each split fewer fitting sites by adding `fitting <- fitting |> filter(site_id %in% sample(unique(site_id), 30))` after the line that sets `fitting`. Does the lowest point move to smaller or larger trees, and why should less data change where it lies?
